She takes her sealskin off like a coat and walks up the beach. What she cannot do is change back without it.

Selkie is simply the old word for seal in Orkney and Shetland. One of these stories was written down in the 1850s from a woman speaking aloud in Shetland. Those islands lost a great many people to the sea and often never got the bodies back, and saying somebody had gone to live with the seal folk was a kinder thing to hold on to.

Look for the sealskin lying open on a rock with nobody inside it.

A nobleman wrote about a strange beast in the mountains in 1233. A monk mentioned creatures called nekomata in 1331. Neither of them said a word about two tails.

That came later. By the 1700s artists in Japan were drawing the nekomata as an old house cat standing up on its back legs in a dim room, with a napkin knotted round its head, dancing. That is the one in the book. It is a very good idea and somebody made it up.

If you have a cat, you already know the hour.

A Norwegian bishop called Erik Pontoppidan put the kraken in a book about his country in the 1750s. He said it was the largest living thing there is, round and flat and covered in arms, and so wide across that fishermen mistook its back for an island.

The real danger was not being eaten. It was the whirlpool it made going back down.

There is an older Norse sea monster called the hafgufa, and the two got muddled together. In 2023 scientists said the hafgufa sounds like a real whale. Some whales lie still with their mouths wide open and let the fish swim in, and nobody had even seen one do that until 2011.

The baku has the trunk of an elephant, the paws of a tiger, the tail of an ox and the ears of a rhinoceros.

It came to Japan from China a long time ago. In a Japanese book from the early 1600s it is simply a strange animal and it does not eat anything at all. By 1791 there is a printed picture of one devouring a nightmare, and after that children were taught to wake up and say, baku, eat this dream. You could buy a pillow with a baku on it.

And here is a true thing. Baku is also the ordinary modern Japanese word for a tapir.

The oldest unicorn in Greek writing comes from a writer named Ctesias about two thousand four hundred years ago. He described wild animals in India with a single horn, a white body, a dark red head and blue eyes.

Much later, people in Europe believed a unicorn's horn could make poisoned water safe to drink. Long twisty horns were sold as unicorn horns and they were worth a great deal. They were really tusks from narwhals, which are whales. In the 1600s the King of Denmark had a throne made from them, and you can still see it in a castle in Copenhagen.

Under the royal hill in Krakow there is a cave, and in summer you can walk into it.

A Polish bishop wrote this story down more than eight hundred years ago. Something lived down there and demanded cattle every single week. The king's sons got rid of it by stuffing a beast full of burning sulfur and leaving it out as dinner. In the oldest telling, that is the whole trick.

The famous ending, where a shoemaker called Skuba thinks of the idea and the dragon drinks the river until it bursts, was added in 1597. That is four hundred years after the story starts.

One of those cows is not behaving the way a cow behaves.

Norwegian trolls are enormous, slow and not at all clever. Long hooked noses, and quite a few of them have more than one head.

The important thing about a troll is that it cannot be caught outside in daylight. The first ray of morning sun turns a troll to stone, permanently. That is how the old stories explain the strange lumps of rock all over the Norwegian mountains. Every oddly shaped boulder up there is a troll who was too slow getting home.

Some have been standing still so long that whole trees have grown on their backs.

If you visit the Australian bush, somebody may warn you about drop bears. Big, heavy, orange fur, waiting up in the gum trees to drop onto whatever walks underneath.

The best protection, you will be told, is to wear forks in your hair or spread Vegemite behind your ears.

None of it is true, and that is the whole point. Drop bears are a joke Australians tell visitors. The Australian Museum even has a page about them with a pretend science name. In 2012 a real scientist published a joke paper about tracking drop bears with satellites.

The forks in her hair will not help. Nothing will.

A griffin has the body of a lion and the head and wings of an eagle, and it is very old indeed. People in the Near East were making pictures of griffins more than five thousand years ago.

The Greek historian Herodotus wrote down a story that far away in the north, griffins guarded gold, and a people with one eye each kept trying to steal it. Another Greek writer had heard that griffins have spots like a leopard.

Much later, rich people in Europe drank from cups that were supposed to be griffin claws. One of them is in the British Museum. The claw is really a horn from a cow or a buffalo, set in silver.

The gold is under its feet. It is not sharing.

In Bavaria they will tell you the woods are full of these. A rabbit head, a squirrel body, deer antlers, pheasant wings, and sometimes a fang. They will offer to take you out at night with a sack and a candle to catch one.

It is a joke, and it has been one for a very long time. What people actually did was stitch dead animals together and sell them to visitors as real. You can still see a whole cabinet of them in a museum in Munich.

But here is the odd bit. Those old pictures of rabbits with horns may have been drawn from life. There is a real illness that makes rabbits grow hard lumps like horns on their heads.

On old farms in Denmark and Sweden, a small man in gray wool and a red cap did all the work nobody ever saw. He fed the animals on time. He kept things in order. In return he got one bowl of porridge at Christmas with butter on top.

One farmer hid the butter underneath instead. The nisse thought he had been cheated, lost his temper completely, and did something dreadful to the cow. Then he ate down to the bottom of the bowl, found the butter, and felt awful. So he went and stole a cow from the next farm to replace it.

In Sweden he is called the tomte, and people there were writing about him in the 1300s.

A Korean book from 1589 names this one, and all it says about how it looks is that it looked like a bear. The metal eating turns up in a much later book.

The story goes that it started tiny, rolled out of leftover rice, and somebody fed it a sewing needle. It ate the needle. Then the scissors. Then every knife in the house, and then the spears the soldiers threw at it, and each mouthful made it bigger.

Nobody could kill it, which is what most people say the name means. Cannot be killed.

The pincushion is where it all started.

The sirens in old Greek stories did not have fish tails. For hundreds of years Greek artists showed them as birds with women's heads.

Then, about thirteen hundred years ago, a book written in England gave sirens the tails of fish. It is the oldest book known to do that.

In the Middle Ages mermaids were carved in churches holding a comb and a mirror. There is one on an old wooden seat in the church at Zennor in Cornwall, carved in the 1400s. People there tell of a mermaid who came up beside a ship and politely asked the sailors to lift their anchor, because it was blocking the door of her house.

A writer called Yamaoka Genrin put this one in a book in 1686, and his book only explains where the creature came from.

Artists in the 1700s are the ones who decided what it looked like. They drew him small, about the size of a child, with a mop of hair and a tongue far longer than any tongue needs to be. He creeps into the bathroom after everyone has gone to bed and licks the tub clean.

People tell it now as a reason to scrub the bath properly. The old book did not. It was simply explaining how a creature made of grime might make a living.

The one clean stripe. He has started already.

In County Durham in the north of England they still sing a song about this one.

A young man went fishing on a Sunday instead of going to church, and he pulled up something horrible. He dropped it down a well so he would not have to think about it. It grew. By the time he came home again it was long enough to coil itself right around a hill, and it was working its way through the sheep.

The song was written in 1867 and people up there have been singing it ever since. The story is much older than the song, though nobody wrote it down until 1785.

The hill has a stripe worn all the way around it. Something big has been sitting there.

Around two thousand four hundred and fifty years ago the Greek historian Herodotus wrote about the phoenix. He had only ever seen pictures of it. Shaped like an eagle, with feathers partly gold and partly red.

People in Egypt told him it came there only once every five hundred years. They said that when its father died, the phoenix made a big ball of sweet smelling myrrh and laid its father inside, then carried him from Arabia to the temple of the sun in Egypt.

There is no fire in his story. A Roman writer later said a new phoenix grew from a tiny worm. The burning version came hundreds of years after Herodotus.

The Classic of Mountains and Seas gives this one a single line. It eats elephants, and after three years it spits out the bones.

An older Chinese poem asks the obvious question, which is how a snake that swallows an elephant is supposed to manage afterward. A scholar named Guo Pu, writing in the three hundreds, decided it was probably a very large python.

People in China still use a saying about the ba snake swallowing the elephant, and they use it about anybody who wants far more than they can possibly handle.

The elephant's back feet are still outside.

A gumiho is a fox that has lived a very long time. Long enough to grow nine tails, and long enough to learn how to take a human shape.

In Korean stories she usually appears as a young woman, and the trouble is that nobody can tell. There is almost always one small slip that gives her away. A tail showing under the hem of a skirt. A shadow on the wall that is the wrong shape.

Nine tailed foxes turn up right across East Asia, in Chinese and Japanese stories too, but the Korean gumiho has her own long history and her own rules.

Check the shadow, not the person.

High in the Alps, farmers and shepherds described this animal for three hundred years, though never in quite the same way. A cat's face. Two clawed front legs, and then nothing but snake for the rest of it.

A Swiss naturalist collected eyewitness accounts in 1814, including one from a village schoolteacher. He believed them enough to offer a large reward to anybody who brought him one. Nobody ever did.

There is a famous photograph of a tatzelwurm from 1934, and it is almost certainly a model somebody built and propped on a rock.

Two legs at the front. Look for where the other two ought to be.

The word is German. Poltern means to make a racket and Geist means ghost, so a poltergeist is a noisy ghost.

It is the only monster in the book that nobody has ever seen, because there is nothing there to see. What people report is the effect. Cupboard doors banging, dishes sliding off shelves, furniture moving about in an empty room, knocking inside the walls at night.

Reports like this go back hundreds of years, all over Europe, and the word crossed into English in 1838.

Whatever else is going on, a poltergeist is somebody else's mess. You cannot spot it. Watch the crockery instead.

Ask anybody in Czechia about the vodník and they will describe the same man. Small, green coat, sitting on a willow branch over the mill pond with a pipe in his mouth. The left tail of his coat drips, and it never stops dripping.

Down under the water he keeps a whole dresser of little pots turned upside down, and there is a soul trapped under every one of them.

It sounds cheerful now. It was not meant to be. Parents told it to keep children away from deep water and fast mill wheels, which really did kill people. A Czech poet put him into a famous poem in 1853.

Count the pots. Now count the little faces peeking out underneath them.

This is the least frightening monster in the book and possibly in the world.

He appears in a cheap Japanese picture book from 1779. He does not chase you, curse you or eat anything. He offers you tofu. Three years later he turns up again, this time in a tofu cookbook.

One researcher has suggested that a tofu seller invented him in order to sell tofu. If that is right, he may be one of the oldest advertising mascots anybody can point to.

He is dressed like a street seller. He is still working. Here he is.

Look for the leaf shape stamped into the tofu.

Ancient Egyptians spent about seventy days preparing a body so that it would last forever. They took the organs out and kept them in four stone jars. The brain was pulled out through the nose and thrown away, because nobody thought it was worth keeping. The heart was left exactly where it was, since Egyptians believed that was where a person did all their thinking.

Then came the wrapping, layer after layer of linen.

Real mummies are real people, and museums today treat them with a great deal more respect than the old films ever did. The monster who lurches about in bandages was invented by Hollywood.

This is where the lanterns at Halloween come from.

In the Irish story Jack was a mean and clever man who tricked his way out of trouble so often that when he finally died there was nowhere left that would have him. He was sent away with a single burning coal to light his path, so he hollowed out a turnip and put the coal inside it, and he has been walking ever since.

People in Ireland and Scotland carved turnips and swedes. In England they used beets. Pumpkins came later, when Irish families arrived in North America and found something far bigger and much easier to hollow out.

France in the 1500s took werewolves extremely seriously. There were real trials, with judges and witnesses and written records. One of them ended with a man called Gilles Garnier being burned at the stake in the 1570s.

What people believed was that a person could change shape and run through the woods on four legs. The French name simply means wolf man, and nearly every country in Europe has its own version of him.

The full moon is the part everybody remembers now. In the older stories the change could come at any time, and it was often blamed on a magic belt or a wolf skin.

Eyebrows that meet in the middle, and a hat running away down the lane by itself.

This one comes from a story written by Washington Irving in 1820, called The Legend of Sleepy Hollow. In it the horseman is the ghost of a soldier who lost his head to a cannonball during the American War of Independence, and every night he rides out looking for it. He chases a nervous schoolteacher named Ichabod Crane through the woods and throws his pumpkin at him.

Irving did not invent the idea. He took it from far older German stories about a wild headless rider, which had been told for centuries and which he had read in a translation by Walter Scott.

Listen for hoofbeats when there is no horse in sight.

Almost every country has one. In Spain he is El Coco. Across Latin America he is El Cucuy. In parts of Europe he is the Sack Man, who carries children off in a bag. In Scotland he is the bogle.

He has no fixed shape at all, and that is rather the point of him. He is whatever a particular child is most afraid of, waiting wherever the light does not quite reach.

Grown ups have been using him to get children to behave for hundreds of years, which probably says more about grown ups than it does about monsters.

In this drawing he is under the bed, and he is more frightened than you are.

Greek stories say there are goblins living under the ground, and they have one job. They are sawing through the trunk of the giant tree that holds the whole world up.

They saw all year. Then at Christmas they get bored and come up to be a nuisance for twelve days. When they climb back down, the tree has healed over and they have to start again.

A scholar named Leo Allatius wrote about them in 1645.

The best part is how you stop one. Hang a colander by the door. A kallikantzaros has to count every hole, and it cannot say the number three, so it counts one two, one two, until the sun comes up.

Krampus walks with Saint Nicholas through the mountain villages of Austria and southern Germany. Nicholas brings the presents. Krampus brings the noise.

He wears a mask carved out of wood and a heavy coat of fur, and the bells strapped across his back are the loudest thing in the whole valley. People have been doing this since at least the 1600s.

Almost everything you may have heard about him being thousands of years old was invented much later by people who wanted a grander story. The real one is better. A village, a dark night in early December, and something enormous coming up the lane, ringing.

The birch twigs. He is holding them like a bunch of flowers.

A German bishop wrote her name down around a thousand years ago, and he was not being kind about it. He called her a witch that common foolishness believed in, and in his version she rides through the night at the head of a crowd of spirits.

The feather bed came much later. That is from the Brothers Grimm, who printed her story in 1812. A girl falls down a well, works hard for an old woman in the world underneath, and is told to shake out the quilt until the feathers fly.

Up above, people look out of the window and say that it is snowing.

One feather has not fallen yet.

Grýla appears in Icelandic writing in the 1200s, in lists of troll women. One saga has a man boasting that he is coming like Grýla, with fifteen tails down his back.

For the first four hundred years she has nothing whatever to do with Christmas. That only begins in poems from the 1600s. A poet in the east of Iceland gave her three heads, with three eyes in each of them. She also got six ears, a nose like a curled ram's horn, and a sack for carrying children.

Her husband Leppalúði turns up in the same poems. He mostly stays in bed, and he is no help whatsoever.

This belongs to Glamorgan in the south of Wales, and it is not really about the horse.

A group arrives at your door with a horse skull under a white sheet, covered in ribbons, with a jaw that clacks. Then they sing at you in Welsh, making up rude verses on the spot, and you have to sing back and beat them. The contest is called the pwnco. If the people in the house run out of rhymes first, they have to open the door and feed everybody.

The first written account is from around 1800. It very nearly died out, and now it is spreading again.

The eyes. Somebody has used bottle glass.

People will tell you that Jack Frost comes out of old Norse stories. He does not. There is nobody of that name anywhere in them. Somebody stuck two real Norse names together a long time ago, and it has been repeated ever since.

What actually happened is that English people fell into the habit of calling anything ordinary Jack, the cold weather included. He is already in print in 1730, in a little book about Christmas, taking somebody by the nose.

So he is about three hundred years old, which is younger than half the book and a great deal older than the stories about him.

The ferns on the glass. He is still drawing them.

In Sweden and Norway the Christmas goat is now a small thing made of straw and tied with a red ribbon, and it sits on the table looking harmless.

It used to be much bigger news. In old church plays the goat was the devil, and Saint Nicholas was the one who tamed him. Then, all through the 1800s, the goat became the one who turned up with the gifts. The first time anybody wrote that down was in 1807, at a house in Sweden.

Nobody has ever explained why it had to be a goat.

The parties he turned up at got so rowdy that in 1726 the police master of Copenhagen banned the lot of them.
